conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. You were brought in because of a fever. Do you remember that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Felt warm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. Your white blood cell count was high, which means your body is fighting something. We think it’s a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I’ve had those before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and this one is caused by a tough bacteria called Pseudomonas. It’s resistant to many antibiotics, so we’re using one called cefepime through your IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we caught it early. You’re not showing signs of serious illness, and your lungs and heart look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I feel okay now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your urine culture. It grew Pseudomonas and another bacteria, but the team thinks only Pseudomonas needs treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why not both?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because the other one might just be contamination. You’re improving, so we don’t need to treat everything that grows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back clean—no bacteria in the blood. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So infection is only in urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And your breathing is stable. We’ll keep supporting your oxygen through the trach and continue the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray of your right hip today because you pointed to it as painful. No new fracture. The osteonecrosis is still there, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hurts more sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving acetaminophen for that. It’s the safest option with your other conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re halfway through your antibiotic course. Fever is gone, white count is coming down. That’s progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a CT scan tomorrow to see why you keep getting UTIs. Could be a stone or something structural.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Like a kidney stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It might explain the repeat infections. We’ll check that and see if a urologist needs to get involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your GJ tube was successfully exchanged today. It was due, and the old one had shifted into the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could have caused blockage or poor feeding. The new one is placed correctly in the jejunum. You can keep getting your feeds as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. You have a 6 mm stone in the right ureter, near the bladder. It’s not blocking anything now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it need to come out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not urgently. But it might be why you keep getting infections. We’re referring you to urology for follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I drink more water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that helps. But with your feeding tube, we’ll make sure your fluids are adjusted properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve now completed your 7-day IV antibiotic course. Your labs look much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m done with IV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No oral antibiotics needed. The infection is cleared. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re ready to go back to your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. When?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably day after tomorrow. We’ll make sure everything is set for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go back to your care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I see urology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve referred you. They’ll check if the stone needs treatment to prevent more infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my HIV meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue exactly as before—Darunavir, ritonavir, Truvada. And your prophylaxis for infections: atovaquone and azithromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Seizure meds too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Keppra twice a day. And citalopram for mood, Ativan if anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Acetaminophen for hip pain. No NSAIDs—they’re not safe with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also saw your bladder wall is thickened, which suggests chronic irritation. That’s another reason to follow up with urology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: From the stone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Or from long-term catheter use. They’ll evaluate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just—am I safe going back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Infection is treated, pain is managed, and your feeding tube is working. Just keep up with your fluids and follow up with urology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sister will be contacted before discharge. She’s listed as your contact.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your trach care and oxygen will continue as before. The facility has the orders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send a note to your infectious disease clinic. They’ll want to know about the resistant Pseudomonas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’ve seen that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and they’ll help monitor for recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your hip pain. Keep using acetaminophen. If it worsens, let your team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And no changes to your feeding—continue tube feeds at goal rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The transport team will get you ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay hydrated and keep up with your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your facility gets all the updates.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And if you develop fever or pain again, they’ll know to check your urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Have a safe trip back.
